message.content:
A large language model (LLM) request is not a single “lookup.” It is a sequence of transformations: text → tokens → embeddings → many transformer layers (attention + feed-forward/MoE) → logits → sampled token → detokenized text. In a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, the feed-forward part is replaced by a router that selects a small subset of experts per token. The hard engineering questions are where those experts live (GPU vs CPU), how their weights are accessed, and how that affects latency, bandwidth, memory capacity, and correctness.

Below is a detailed end-to-end explanation, with a concrete example, GPU-resident vs CPU-resident expert comparison, trade-offs, and practical tuning guidance.

---

## 1. End-to-end request lifecycle

### 1.1 Tokenization

The raw prompt is converted into token IDs by a tokenizer:

- Common algorithms: BPE, SentencePiece, Unigram, WordPiece.
- The tokenizer has a vocabulary, e.g. 32k–200k tokens.
- Special tokens may be added: BOS, EOS, system/user/assistant markers,
